newsitem.title: USA: FBI lab under attack in Oklahoma bomb trial.
newsitem.headline: FBI lab under attack in Oklahoma bomb trial.

text.p: An FBI chemist testified on Tuesday that the crime lab used to analyse Oklahoma City bomb evidence was contaminated with explosives residue, a charge defence lawyers hope will blow a hole in the government's case against Timothy McVeigh.

Frederic Whitehurst, an FBI agent and chemist whose complaints sparked an internal investigation into the crime lab, said he found the contamination in May 1995, just weeks after the federal building was bombed killing 168 people.
Whitehurst said the contamination, found in four or five spots dotted around the lab, meant that findings by the lab were unreliable.

"If we're processing evidence and we're contaminated ourselves then you don't know whether our finding of explosives material on a piece of evidence is a result of our contamination of the evidence ourselves or if the explosive residue was on the evidence before it got to us," he said.
Jurors watched intently as Whitehurst said that other FBI agents who had handled and analysed explosives residue had not been officially qualified to do so.

Also paying close attention was McVeigh, who has pleaded not guilty to the devastating attack. If found guilty, the Gulf War veteran faces the death penalty. His defence team is expected to wrap up its case this week.
Whitehurst was a star witness for the defence, which is fighting to dismantle a carefully constructed government case linking McVeigh to the April 19, 1995 Oklahoma City bombing.

The FBI whistleblower testified on Tuesday that FBI agent Steven Burmeister kept small quantities of certain explosives on hand at the lab to use in testing and said this could result in lab contamination.

He said he was baffled when Burmeister testified for for the prosecution that crystals of ammonium nitrate had been found embedded in a panel the government says came from the truck used in the bombing. The panel, a crucial piece of evidence found near the bombing site, is believed to have been left out in the rain, Whitehurst said -- exposure that normally would obliterate any ammonium nitrate traces.
"I don't know how that ammonium nitrate survived if it went through a rainstorm. I don't know how it could be on that evidence. It doesn't make sense to me," Whitehurst said.

He also testified he was told by FBI agent David Williams that the panel had been found by a private citizen instead of trained investigators, which could call into question the "chain of custody" standard for ensuring that all evidence is guaranteed free of contamination.

Whitehurst quoted Williams as telling him: "We had a problem with the chain of custody and we're not going to use it." But Williams, who testified earlier on Tuesday, said he could not remember that conversation.

Whitehurst's testimony appeared damaging for the prosecution, although he did admit under cross-examination that he was not personally familiar with all the data on the ammonium nitrate, which the government claims was the chief ingredient of the bomb.

He said he had formed his opinion based on the information available to him and admitted that there could be factors involved about which he was not aware. Nevertheless, his testimony dovetailed nicely with defence attempts to paint the FBI and government investigators as incompetent and overeager.

Williams, who had been criticised by name in a Justice Department report on the crime laboratory, testified earlier on Tuesday that there was no single person in charge of evidence collection at the scene, suggesting the evidence against McVeigh could be unreliable.
